title: Macro security and .xlsm files
summary: Macros can do anything you can, so Excel switches them off until you say so. Save macro workbooks as .xlsm, enable content only in files you trust, and unblock files from the internet in their Properties, or keep them in a trusted location.
objectives: Explain why Excel disables macros, and what a macro could do.
Choose the right file type: .xlsx, .xlsm, .xlsb or .xlam.
Enable macros with the yellow bar, and know when not to.
Unblock a file from the internet, and use trusted locations.

slides.h: A macro can do anything you can
p: VBA can open, change and delete files, send email, and run other programs, with your permissions. That’s what makes it useful, and why a macro from a stranger is dangerous.
Most macro viruses arrive as an email attachment or a download.
So Excel opens macro workbooks with the macros **switched off**.
You decide, file by file, whether to switch them on.
In real life: got an “invoice.xlsm” from a supplier she’d never heard of. She deleted it without opening it.

p: A normal workbook, .xlsx, can’t hold macros at all. Workbooks with macros are .xlsm. A .xlsb is a smaller, faster binary file that can hold macros too, and a .xlam is an add-in.
The **m** in .xlsm stands for macro-enabled.
An .xlsx can never contain code, so it’s safe to open from anyone.
Your own macros everywhere: the Personal Macro Workbook (Lesson 1.4).
In real life: keeps two files: the .xlsm tool that does the work, and the .xlsx report it sends to Farah.

slides.h: Save as .xlsx and the code is gone
p: Add a macro to an .xlsx and press Save, and Excel warns you: the VB project can’t be saved in a macro-free workbook. Click Yes and the macros are thrown away. Click No and choose Excel Macro-Enabled Workbook.
**No** takes you to Save As: pick **Excel Macro-Enabled Workbook (*.xlsm)**.
**Yes** saves without the code. It’s gone for good.
Check the file name ends in .xlsm before you close.
In real life: clicked Yes. Arjun’s macro vanished, and so did her afternoon.

lecture.title: The yellow bar and the red bar

p: Open a macro workbook and Excel shows a yellow bar: Macros have been disabled. If you know the file and who made it, click Enable Content. Excel remembers that file as a trusted document on this computer.
The workbook opens normally; only the macros are off.
**Enable Content** switches them on and trusts the file next time.
Not sure who made it? Leave it disabled and ask.
In real life: opens Arjun’s tool every morning. She clicked Enable Content once, the first day.

slides.h: SECURITY RISK: blocked from the internet
p: Files downloaded or opened from email carry a mark saying they came from the internet. For those, Excel blocks macros completely: a red bar, and no Enable Content button. If you trust it, close the file, right-click it in File Explorer, Properties, tick Unblock, OK, and open it again.
The red bar means Microsoft blocked it: there’s no button to override it inside Excel.
Unblock only files you expected, from people you know.
Saving it into a **trusted location** also works (next slide).
In real life: emailed his tool to the Kochi branch. They saw the red bar and thought it was broken. Now his email says how to unblock it.

slides.h: The Trust Center and trusted locations
p: Developer › Macro Security opens the Trust Center. Leave it on Disable VBA macros with notification: that’s what gives you the yellow bar. Folders added under Trusted Locations open macro files with no questions asked.
**Disable with notification** (the default) is the right setting for nearly everyone.
**Never** choose Enable VBA macros: every file’s code would run, including bad ones.
A trusted location is good for your own tools folder; never for Downloads.
In real life: keeps his tools in C:\Nilgiri\Tools, a trusted location. They open with macros on.

modules.code:
Sub MarkDispatched()
' Marks every order as dispatched today, for the dispatch register
    Dim r As Long
    With Worksheets("Orders")
        .Range("I1").Value = "Dispatched"
        .Range("I1").Font.Bold = True
        For r = 2 To .Cells(.Rows.Count, 1).End(xlUp).Row
            .Cells(r, 9).Value = "Yes"
        Next r
    End With
End Sub

points: Macros can do anything you can, so Excel opens them **disabled**.
Save macro workbooks as **.xlsm** (or .xlsb, .xlam); .xlsx throws the code away.
Yellow bar: **Enable Content** for files you trust. Red bar: the file came from the internet; **unblock** it in its Properties.
Keep the Trust Center on **Disable with notification**; use **trusted locations** for your own tools.
recap.cheat: Macros = .xlsm; enable only what you trust; red bar → Properties › Unblock.
